questions.explanation: Simple harmonic motion is exactly the motion whose acceleration is proportional to displacement and directed back toward equilibrium, a = -ω²x, with ω the angular frequency. questions.explanation: At a turning point the mass momentarily stops, so v = 0, and the spring is stretched or compressed by the full amplitude, so a = -ω²A has its largest magnitude there. At equilibrium the displacement is zero, the spring exerts no force, a = 0, and the speed is at its maximum because all of the energy is kinetic. Since v² = ω²(A² - x²) and the right-hand side is largest at x = 0 and vanishes at x = ±A, the two quantities are in antiphase, and energy is constantly shuttling between them across the cycle.
questions.hint: Use v² = ω²(A² - x²) and a = -ω²x and see when each one reaches its extreme.

questions.explanation: The damping force always opposes the velocity, so the work it does over any stretch of a cycle is negative, and mechanical energy is transferred irreversibly to the surroundings on every pass. The stored energy therefore falls cycle by cycle and the envelope of the motion decays, in the light-damping limit like e^(-ct). Nothing is given back because the force is not conservative, it is a one-way transfer into heat in the dashpot. Over many cycles the amplitude can become very small, while the timing of the surviving oscillations is barely affected at all.
questions.hint: A force opposing the motion always does negative work, and it is not conservative.

questions.explanation: The drive does its most efficient work when its period matches the natural period, because then each push arrives at the same phase of the motion as the push before it and the work done per cycle accumulates instead of cancelling. At 4.0 rad/s the two periods coincide and the amplitude grows until damping balances the input. The response is largest near the middle of a sweep rather than at its edge, so a setting that merely happens to be the largest one tried cannot be the resonant one. Damping does not vanish at a particular frequency, and the stiffness of a spring is fixed by its material and geometry.
questions.hint: Ask whether the drive pushes hardest when the mass is moving fastest, and when that happens.

Because both curves approach the axis, the oscillation is losing amplitude, which is the signature of damping. The equilibrium position is the fixed midline the trace oscillates about, so it would be a horizontal line rather than a falling pair. Velocity is a sine wave leading the displacement by a quarter cycle, and energy never goes negative at all.

questions.explanation: The amplitude-against-frequency curve of a driven damped oscillator has a single resonance peak, and for light damping that peak sits at the undamped natural frequency ω₀ = √(k/m), which here is close to 6.0 rad/s. The peak lands at ω₀ rather than above it because the drive delivers energy most efficiently when it arrives in step with the motion, and the exact solution puts it at √(ω₀² - 2c²), a shift too small to notice with light damping. A dip would be antiresonance, which a single-degree-of-freedom amplitude response does not exhibit.
questions.hint: The peak of the response sits at, or just below, the undamped natural frequency.
